facts.statehood_note: Before statehood the land was Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory. A 1905 plan for a separate Indian-led state called Sequoyah was turned down by the United States, and the two areas joined as one state.
facts.motto: Labor Omnia Vincit (Latin for "work conquers all things")
facts.name_origin: From two Choctaw words: okla ("people") and humma ("red").

government.chambers: Oklahoma Senate (48 senators, 4-year terms, half elected every two years) and Oklahoma House of Representatives (101 members, 2-year terms). The Legislature meets each year from the first Monday in February to the last Friday in May.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; no person may serve as governor for more than eight years in all, whether or not the years are in a row). The governor leads the executive branch and can call the Legislature into special meetings.
government.courts: Oklahoma has two top courts: the Oklahoma Supreme Court (9 justices) hears civil cases, and the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals (5 judges) hears criminal cases. There are 77 district courts.
government.local: 77 counties; communities are organized as towns or cities (a city must have at least 1,000 people).
government.constitution: Voters approved the Oklahoma Constitution on September 17, 1907, and it took effect when Oklahoma became the 46th state on November 16, 1907.
government.kid_line: "All persons have the inherent right to life, liberty, the pursuit of happiness, and the enjoyment of the gains of their own industry." (Oklahoma Constitution, Article II, Section 2)

long_ago.nation: Spiro people (Caddoan-speaking ancestors of the Caddo, Wichita, and related nations)
long_ago.about: Spiro on the Arkansas River became a permanent town around AD 800 and was a major center until about 1450. Its leaders traded from the Gulf of Mexico to the Great Lakes and the Virginia coast, and its 12 mounds held one of the largest collections of ancient art in the United States.
Wichita ancestors lived on the eastern Great Plains for at least 2,000 years and became farmers. Southern Plains farming villages grew corn, beans, squash, and tobacco and also hunted bison and deer.
The Caddo built ritual centers with platform mounds around plazas by AD 800. The Caddo Nation of Oklahoma descends from this culture.
Plains Apache people came onto the Southern Plains between 1300 and 1500, and the Kiowa came from the Rocky Mountains. The two nations lived side by side and shared many ways of life.
The Comanche came from the Great Basin onto the Southern Plains by the early 1700s, after they got horses.
The Osage moved into northeastern Oklahoma by 1796.

today.about: Removed to Indian Territory on the Trail of Tears; Wilma Mankiller became its first woman Principal Chief in 1985.
The first of the Five Tribes forced to move, starting in 1831 under the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek.
Gave up its homeland under the Treaty of Pontotoc (1832) and moved to Indian Territory in 1837.
Forced out of its homeland by the U.S. military in 1837; one of the Five Tribes.
Removed from Florida over almost twenty years after the Treaty of Payne's Landing (1832).
Ballerina Maria Tallchief grew up on the Osage reservation and was a proud Osage citizen.
Descends from the Caddoan mound-building culture of the region.
Descendants of the Wichita, whose ancestors farmed the Southern Plains for thousands of years.

first_peoples.today_note: Oklahoma has 38 federally recognized tribes. Most were forced to move here from other places in the 1800s, when the U.S. government made the area Indian Territory.
sites: Spiro Mounds Archaeological Center (Spiro), 12 mounds of a great Caddoan trading town
Sequoyah's Cabin, the log home Sequoyah built in 1829
Honey Springs Battlefield, a National Historic Landmark
Tallgrass Prairie Preserve (Osage County), home to about 1,800 bison

history.event: Ice Age hunters in what is now Harper County painted a bison skull (the Cooper Bison Skull), the oldest known painted object in North America.
Spiro, a Caddoan town on the Arkansas River, grows into a great trading and religious center.
The Spanish expedition of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado passes through the land.
The Louisiana Purchase puts most of the land under U.S. control.
The U.S. Army builds Fort Gibson and Fort Towson.
Congress passes the Indian Removal Act. The Choctaw are the first of the Five Tribes forced to move west, starting in 1831.
About 16,000 Cherokee people are forced west on the Trail of Tears; about 4,000 die on the way. The Muscogee (Creek) and Chickasaw also move in 1837.
About 8,000 to 10,000 Black people are enslaved in Indian Territory, brought west by enslavers among the Five Tribes. The Five Tribes sign treaties with the Confederacy.

The Cherokee National Council passes a law freeing enslaved people. On July 17, Union forces win the Battle of Honey Springs; the First Kansas Colored Volunteers, one of the first Black regiments in the Union army, fight there, and Cherokee and Muscogee soldiers fight on both sides.
On June 23, Cherokee leader Stand Watie surrenders, the last Confederate general to do so.
New treaties with the Five Tribes end slavery, set out citizenship rights for Freedmen, give up western lands to the United States, and let railroads cross Indian lands.
The Medicine Lodge Treaty assigns new reservations to Plains nations such as the Kiowa and Comanche.
Bass Reeves, who had been enslaved, becomes a deputy U.S. marshal in Indian Territory.
Oklahoma becomes the 46th state on November 16, 1907.

trailblazers.name: Sequoyah
trailblazers.text: Sequoyah created a written symbol for each sound in the Cherokee language and finished his syllabary by 1821, so Cherokee people could read and write their own language. He moved to what is now Oklahoma and built a log cabin there in 1829.

trailblazers.name: Bass Reeves
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved, Bass Reeves became a deputy U.S. marshal in Indian Territory in 1875 and served about 32 years, until statehood. He said he arrested more than 3,000 people who broke federal laws.

trailblazers.name: Maria Tallchief
trailblazers.text: Born in Fairfax, Maria Tallchief became the first American prima ballerina and danced as the star of the New York City Ballet. She was famous for the magic bird in Firebird (1949) and was proud of her Osage identity all her life.

trailblazers.name: Ada Lois Sipuel Fisher
trailblazers.text: In 1946 the University of Oklahoma law school turned her away because of her race. She sued, and her case reached the U.S. Supreme Court in 1948; she entered the law school in 1949, became a lawyer, and later served on the university's Board of Regents.

trailblazers.name: Clara Luper
trailblazers.text: A history teacher for 41 years, Clara Luper led Oklahoma City's NAACP Youth Council in a sit-in at the Katz Drug Store lunch counter in August 1958. It led to more peaceful protests, marches, and voter drives across the city.

trailblazers.name: Wilma Mankiller
trailblazers.text: In 1985 Wilma Mankiller became the first woman Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. She built water lines, health clinics, and job programs, and she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1998.

waters: Lake Texoma (largest lake by volume; most Oklahoma lakes are made by dams)
geography.regions: Oklahoma has mountains and forested highlands in the east (Ozark and Ouachita), part of the Coastal Plain, and plains in the center and west, rising to the High Plains of the Panhandle; it has 11 ecoregions, more than any other state.

ecosystems.name: Tallgrass prairie
ecosystems.about: Only about 4% of tallgrass prairie remains intact. The Tallgrass Prairie Preserve in Osage County, about 39,650 acres, is the largest protected piece in the world, and its bison herd has grown from 300 in 1993 to about 1,800.

ecosystems.name: Mixed-grass prairie and granite mountains
ecosystems.about: The Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge protects about 60,000 acres of mixed-grass prairie, ancient granite mountains, lakes, and streams, with bison, elk, longhorn cattle, and prairie dogs.

ecosystems.name: Rivers and lakes
ecosystems.about: Most of Oklahoma drains into the Red and Arkansas rivers, and more than 500 named creeks and rivers flow through the state.

science.weather: Most of Oklahoma lies in Tornado Alley, and about 62 tornadoes strike the state in an average year, one of the highest rates in the world. Strong cold fronts can change the weather fast: on November 11, 1911, Oklahoma City went from 83°F to 17°F in one day.
science.resources: Oil and natural gas brought great wealth; Oklahoma is the third-largest producer of natural gas and fifth-largest producer of crude oil in the U.S. Farmers grow wheat (fifth in the nation), cotton, and peanuts, and aviation is a key industry.
science.highlight: Storm science: NOAA's Storm Prediction Center, which issues tornado watches for the whole country, is in Norman at the National Weather Center. In 1948 two Air Force weather officers at Tinker Air Force Base near Oklahoma City successfully predicted a tornado five days after another one hit the base.

g3_ss.title: Oklahoma's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Oklahoma City, Tulsa, and the student's town; learn the Legislature (Senate 48, House 101), the governor, and the two top courts; read Article II, Section 2 together.

g3_ss.title: Oklahoma's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Wichita, Caddo, Kiowa, Comanche, and Osage; learn why 38 nations have governments in Oklahoma today and find the Cherokee, Choctaw, and Chickasaw nations on a map.

g3_ss.title: Oklahoma Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Timeline cards for Sequoyah, Bass Reeves, Maria Tallchief, Clara Luper, and Wilma Mankiller; students write one sentence on how each changed Oklahoma.

g45_ss.title: Oklahoma's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: The Cooper Bison Skull, the Spiro trading center, Plains farming villages, and how horses changed life for the Comanche and Kiowa.

g45_ss.title: Removal and Indian Territory, 1803–1860
g45_ss.plan: Louisiana Purchase, Fort Gibson, the Indian Removal Act, the Trail of Tears and other removals, rebuilding nations in the West, and slavery within Indian Territory.

g45_ss.title: War and Freedom in Indian Territory, 1861–1877
g45_ss.plan: Confederate treaties, Honey Springs and the First Kansas Colored Volunteers, the 1866 treaties and Freedmen citizenship, Medicine Lodge, and Bass Reeves; close with the road to 1907 statehood.

g3_sci.title: Tornado Alley
g3_sci.plan: How thunderstorms form, the difference between a tornado watch and warning, and a family safety plan.

g3_sci.title: Prairie Home
g3_sci.plan: Bison, prairie dogs, and tall grasses; build a prairie food web using the Tallgrass Prairie Preserve and Wichita Mountains.

g3_sci.title: Oklahoma State Symbols in Nature
g3_sci.plan: Observe and sketch the scissor-tailed flycatcher, redbud, Indian blanket, and collared lizard; sort them as plants or animals and describe their habitats.

g45_sci.title: Forecasting Severe Weather
g45_sci.plan: Fronts, temperature drops, and storm data; how the Storm Prediction Center in Norman issues watches, using the 1948 Tinker forecast story.

g45_sci.title: Bringing Back the Bison
g45_sci.plan: Population growth from 300 to about 1,800 bison, graphing herd size, and why only about 4% of tallgrass prairie remains.

g45_sci.title: Oil, Gas, and Rock
g45_sci.plan: How fossil fuels form underground, Oklahoma's oil and gas production, and the state's granite mountains and rose rock.
